newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand seen struggling to keep balanced budget.
newsitem.headline: Thailand seen struggling to keep balanced budget.

text.p: Thailand might not sustain its balanced, deficit-free budget policy after the cabinet approved a planned nine percent budget hike for the 1997/98 (October/September) fiscal year, analysts said on Thursday.
They said the moderate 1.008 trillion baht ($38.8 billion) budget for 1997/98 was planned against a backdrop of a sharply slowing economy and falling government tax revenue this year.
Gross domestic product grew 6.7 percent in 1996 after 8.7 percent in 1995. The economy is projected to expand about 6.8 percent this year, although private analysts expect it to be lower.
The local financial sector has also been hit by billions of dollars in sour loans to the depressed property sector, which is facing a liquidity crunch.
Authorities last month ordered a revamp of the sector and asked financial institutions to raise provisioning to cover sub-standard assets further.

"My impression is the nine percent increase would be excessive if the weak economy continued failing to show signs of recovery by next year,' said Charl Kengchon, an analyst at Thai Farmers Research Center Co Ltd.

The proposed budget hike, which has to go through several rounds of executive and legislative approval before formal adoption in the third quarter of this year, will represent the smallest annual increase in 10 years.

Budget Bureau Director Seree Sukstaporn said on Wednesday the planned increase was based on the current year's reduced 925 billion baht spending, which emerged after a recent government decision to cut its budget.
After nine years of surpluses, analysts said Thailand may fail to register a budget surplus this year .
Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan described the new budget as a conservative figure reflective of anticipated government tax revenue.
The minister said he would strive to maintain Thailand's balanced budget policy adopted by successive governments since the second half of the 1980s.

Desmond Supple, of Barclays de Zoete Wedd Securities Ltd, said: "It's quite encouraging that they are aiming for a moderate budget hike based on the current year's trimmed expenditure... and to avoid a deficit."
Figures released by the finance ministry said the government cash balance posted a monthly deficit in three of the first five months of the current fiscal year as tax collection missed its target.
"There is a big risk of the government failing to meet its balanced budget this year," Supple said.
Kengchon of Thai Farmers Research said he did not see hints of any economic pick-up from latest indicators released by the central bank.

"If the economic slowdown dragged on into next year, it is vital for the government to maintain strict fiscal disciplines. We must ensure that the proposed budget hike does not erode our national coffers," he said.

Kingchon said if the government faced problems of meeting its tax revenue target, a more stringent budget hike should be considered for next year to cover only an expected five percent inflation in 1998.
The economist, however, was not all critical. He said the government may opt to make interim budget cuts next year if tax revenue did not reach projected level.
